title: First appearance of a species in a formation usually marks immigration

fields.label: Label
fields.value: First appearance of a species in a formation usually marks immigration

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When a marine species first appears partway through a formation, the most probable explanation is that it immigrated into that area at that time rather than originated there.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: when we see a species first appearing in any formation, the probability is that it only then first immigrated into that area.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IX, “On the Imperfection of the Geological Record”; section “On the absence of intermediate varieties in any one formation”. Scope: marine fossil species in regional stratigraphic sequences

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch09-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Georeferenced fossil occurrences allow explicit comparison of regional and global first appearances. Preservation and dating biases remain, but standard occupancy and sensitivity analyses can test the probabilistic generalization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For regional first appearances within formations, compare local first-occurrence dates with older occurrences elsewhere and use phylogeographic or occupancy models to classify immigration versus local origination. A majority with prior external records supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Age uncertainty can reverse apparent first appearances.

The true source area may be unsampled.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The immigration test is a spatial query on a single open occurrence database and is practical to run. It can confirm immigration whenever an older external record exists, which is the informative direction. The converse, local origin, is hardly distinguishable from incomplete geographic sampling, so the claim that immigration is the usual explanation stays only partly decidable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For marine species whose first local occurrence is above the base of a formation, test whether older occurrences exist in other regions. A majority with earlier records elsewhere would support immigration as the usual explanation; a majority with no earlier record anywhere, in well-sampled groups, would favor local origin.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Reworking and uncertain correlation can create false earlier occurrences.

Failure to find an older record elsewhere is weak evidence of in-situ origin because most regions are undersampled.

Many species are known from a single basin, so the test has no second locality.
